title: Generative artificial intelligence-supported programming education: Effects on learning performance, self-efficacy and processes
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), specifically ChatGPT, improves programming education outcomes and how it shapes students’ learning processes. The authors focus on four questions: whether GenAI improves programming output quality and knowledge transfer, whether it affects programming self-efficacy, how it changes students’ programming behaviours, and how different behaviour patterns under GenAI relate to academic performance. The study responds to mixed prior findings suggesting that GenAI may improve immediate task performance but may not always support deeper learning.

The intervention was a quasi-experiment in which one group of students used a ChatGPT-based platform (ChatGPT-Next-Web using GPT-3.5-turbo) for self-directed programming learning, while a control group used other Internet resources instead of GenAI. Both groups completed the same Turtle-library programming learning tasks in a standardized computer lab setting. Measures included ratings of programming products across multiple dimensions, pre/post programming self-efficacy surveys, and fine-grained behavioural trace data captured through scripts and analysed with frequency analysis, process mining, and clustering.

Participants were 55 undergraduate Physics Education students at a public university in China. All had prior foundational Python experience but were new to the Python Turtle library. The experimental activity itself lasted 120 minutes, followed by a 40-minute post-test task completed without external resources. The study took place in university computer labs with uniform hardware, and the authors also provided the experimental group with a GenAI user guide to support interaction with the tool.

The main conclusions are that GenAI support improved short-term programming performance and increased self-efficacy, especially in self-regulation and complex programming tasks, but did not improve longer-term knowledge transfer when students later had to work without external resources. Behavioural analyses showed that GenAI-supported learners relied more on information retrieval and copying, whereas control students engaged more in independent coding and code revision. Within the GenAI group, higher-performing students used the tool more critically and interactively, showing greater epistemic agency, while lower-performing students were more likely to copy outputs directly. The authors argue that GenAI can be beneficial for programming education, but only when instructional design discourages over-reliance and supports active cognitive engagement.
